slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
When most people think of Bordeaux, they think first of powerful, elegant red wines. In reality, the range of wine styles produced in Bordeaux is far richer than imagined: from dry reds and whites to the world-class noble-rot sweet wine of Sauternes, to rosés and sparkling wines — Bordeaux covers almost every major wine type.

This course will give you a comprehensive view of Bordeaux's wine-type landscape. We will explore the dominance and stylistic categories of dry red wines, the freshness and complexity of dry whites, the layers and craftsmanship of sweet whites, the history and modern expression of rosés (Clairet and Rosé), and the rise of sparkling wine (Crémant de Bordeaux). Most importantly, we will understand the production methods, quality differences, food-pairing suggestions, and market positioning of each wine type.

Learning Objectives

🍷 Master the Distribution of Red Wine Types

Understand dry red wine's share of production (80%+), key appellations, and stylistic categories

🥂 Appreciate White Wine Diversity

Learn the varietal differences, production characteristics, and flavour profiles of dry and sweet white wines

🍯 Explore Sauternes Noble-Rot Sweet Wine

Discover Sauternes, one of the world's three great noble-rot wine regions, and the magical role of Botrytis cinerea

🌸 Explore Rosé Traditions

Understand the differences and character of Clairet (a historic Bordeaux style) and modern Rosé

✨ Learn About Sparkling Wine Development

Learn the production method, quality standards, and market trends of Crémant de Bordeaux

After completing this course, you will be able to give a comprehensive description of Bordeaux's wine-type system and select the right Bordeaux wine for any occasion and preference.
slides.1.title: Red Wine Types
slides.1.subtitle: Styles and Characteristics of Left and Right Bank Reds
slides.2.title: Red Wine Types and Regional Distribution
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Dry Red Wines
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Bordeaux's flagship product, accounting for over 80% of total production
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Regional Diversity
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Left Bank and Right Bank each have their own character; stylistic differences are pronounced
slides.2.content:
Bordeaux is world-famous for its red wines. Reds from different appellations each have their own character, forming a complete quality hierarchy from everyday drinking wines to top collector bottles.

🏰 Left Bank Red Wine Appellations

Médoc
  • Location: Left bank of the Gironde, north of Bordeaux city
  • Key varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominant, blended with Merlot
  • Wine style: Powerful structure, rich tannins, excellent ageing potential
  • Key appellations: Saint-Julien, Pauillac, Saint-Estèphe, Margaux
  • Quality level: Includes numerous classified growths
Graves
  • Location: Left bank of the Gironde, south of Bordeaux city
  • Soil character: Gravel soils with excellent drainage
  • Wine characteristics: Balanced and elegant, distinct minerality
  • Sub-appellation: Pessac-Léognan is the highest-quality tier
  • Historical standing: One of Bordeaux's oldest appellations

💎 Right Bank Red Wine Appellations

Saint-Émilion
  • Location: Right bank of the Dordogne
  • Key varieties: Merlot dominant, blended with Cabernet Franc
  • Soil types: Limestone plateau and sandy clay
  • Wine style: Elegant and refined, generous fruit character
  • Classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A and B tiers
Pomerol
  • Location: Right bank of the Dordogne, north of Saint-Émilion
  • Key varieties: Merlot dominant (up to 95%)
  • Soil character: Deep clay with iron-rich deposits
  • Wine characteristics: Rich and powerful, silky texture
  • Scarce production: Small area, limited output, high prices
Fronsac
  • Location: Right bank of the Dordogne
  • Variety composition: Merlot, Cabernet Franc
  • Wine character: Excellent value for money; consistent quality
  • Style: Positioned between Saint-Émilion and Pomerol

🍇 Generic Bordeaux Appellations

Bordeaux AOC
  • Coverage: Entire Bordeaux wine region
  • Production share: Approximately 50% of all Bordeaux wines
  • Quality positioning: Entry-level to medium quality
  • Price range: The most accessible Bordeaux wines
  • Drinkability: Enjoyable when young
Bordeaux Supérieur AOC
  • Quality requirements: More stringent than basic Bordeaux AOC
  • Alcohol: Minimum 10.5% vs 10%
  • Ageing requirement: Requires longer ageing period
  • Style uplift: Richer and more structured
slides.2.quiz.question: What is the main characteristic of Bordeaux AOC wines?
slides.2.quiz.options.1: Covers the entire Bordeaux wine region
slides.2.quiz.options.2: Must be aged for at least 5 years
slides.2.quiz.options.3: Can only be produced on the Left Bank
slides.2.quiz.explanation: Bordeaux AOC is the basic-level appellation covering the entire Bordeaux wine region, accounting for approximately 50% of total Bordeaux production. It is the most accessible entry point into Bordeaux wine.
slides.4.title: Service A/B User Guide
slides.5.title: Winemaking Keys: Stainless Steel vs Oak | Noble Rot vs Extraction
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Container Influence
slides.5.highlights.0.content: Stainless steel preserves freshness; oak adds body and spice
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Technique Differences
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Noble rot concentrates sugar and acid; red-wine extraction builds structure
slides.6.title: Service and Food Pairing Checklist (Temperature / Glass / Decanting / Pairing)
slides.6.highlights.0.title: Practical Guide
slides.6.highlights.0.content: Get the temperature and glass right first, and the flavours immediately improve
slides.6.highlights.1.title: Logical Pairing
slides.6.highlights.1.content: Structure pairs with bold food; acidity cuts fat; sweetness matches spicy and salty
slides.6.quiz.question: Which of the following wine type → service strategy pairings is most appropriate?
slides.6.quiz.options.1: Crémant de Bordeaux: 6–8°C, tulip glass, no decanting
slides.6.quiz.options.2: Left Bank red: 12–14°C, small white-wine glass
slides.6.quiz.explanation: Sparkling wine should be served at 6–8°C in a tulip glass without decanting. Noble-rot sweet wines should not be served too warm and generally do not need extended decanting. Structured reds require higher serving temperatures and large glasses.
slides.7.title: White Wines and Special Types
slides.7.subtitle: Dry Whites, Sweet Wines, and Sparkling Wines
slides.8.title: The Diversity of White and Sweet Wines
slides.8.highlights.0.title: Dry White Wines
slides.8.highlights.0.content: Fresh and elegant; blended from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon
slides.8.highlights.1.title: Noble-Rot Sweet Wines
slides.8.highlights.1.content: World-class sweet wines; the masterwork of Sauternes and Barsac
slides.8.content:
Although Bordeaux is celebrated for red wine, its white and sweet wines are equally world-class in quality — particularly the noble-rot sweet wines of Sauternes, often described as liquid gold.

🤍 Dry White Wines

Graves White Wines
  • Variety composition: Sauvignon Blanc 60–80%, Sémillon 20–40%
  • Production style: Stainless steel fermentation for freshness; partial oak ageing
  • Flavour profile: Citrus fruit, cut grass, mineral character
  • Quality level: Pessac-Léognan is the top tier
  • Ageing potential: 3–8 years; premium examples up to 15 years
Pessac-Léognan White Wines
  • Status: Bordeaux's finest dry white wines
  • Production character: Barrel fermentation and oak ageing
  • Style: Rich and complex; creamy texture
  • Aged development: Honey, nuts, smoke aromas
  • International standing: Comparable to top white Burgundy
Entre-Deux-Mers White Wines
  • Location: Between the Gironde and the Dordogne
  • Varietal character: Sauvignon Blanc dominant; fresh fruit aromas
  • Style positioning: Refreshing and easy-drinking; excellent value
  • Serving temperature: 8–10°C; serve well chilled
  • Pairing suggestions: Seafood, salads, goat's cheese

🍯 Sweet Wine Types

Sauternes Noble-Rot Sweet Wine
  • Botrytis effect: Botrytis cinerea concentrates grape sugars
  • Variety composition: Sémillon 80%, Sauvignon Blanc 15%, Muscadelle 5%
  • Flavour profile: Honey, apricot, orange peel, spice
  • Ageing potential: 20–100 years or more
  • World standing: On a par with German Riesling ice wine
Barsac Sweet Wine
  • Geographic relationship: Sub-appellation within Sauternes
  • Style difference: Relatively fresher; higher acidity
  • Soil influence: Limestone soils impart elegance
  • Labelling choice: May be labelled Barsac or Sauternes
  • Typical characteristics: More pronounced floral aromas; a more delicate palate
Other Sweet Wine Appellations
  • Cadillac: Value-for-money sweet wine
  • Loupiac: Semi-sweet to sweet style
  • Sainte-Croix-du-Mont: Traditional sweet wine
  • Cérons: Semi-sweet white wine

⚙️ Production Method Differences

Dry White Wine Production
  • Harvest timing: Moderate ripeness; acidity preserved
  • Fermentation vessel: Stainless steel tank or oak barrel
  • Temperature control: Cool fermentation at 16–20°C
  • Lees contact: Aged on lees for 3–6 months
  • Bottling: 6–12 months after fermentation
Noble-Rot Sweet Wine Production
  • Harvest method: Hand-picking in successive passes (tris), up to 6–10 passes
  • Botrytis conditions: Morning mist + afternoon sunshine — a unique microclimate
  • Sugar concentration: Up to 300–400 g/L
  • Fermentation time: Slow fermentation over weeks to months
  • Oak ageing: New oak barrel ageing for 18–24 months
slides.8.quiz.question: What is the key to producing Sauternes noble-rot sweet wine?
slides.8.quiz.explanation: The key to Sauternes noble-rot sweet wine is infection by Botrytis cinerea, which — under the unique conditions of morning mist and afternoon sunshine — concentrates the sugars and flavour compounds in the grapes.
slides.9.title: Sparkling Wines and Special Wine Types
slides.9.highlights.0.title: Crémant de Bordeaux
slides.9.highlights.0.content: Bordeaux's traditional-method sparkling wine; outstanding quality
slides.9.highlights.1.title: Rosé Wines
slides.9.highlights.1.content: Fresh and elegant; ideal for summer enjoyment
slides.9.content:
Beyond the classic reds, whites, and sweet wines, Bordeaux also produces high-quality sparkling wines and rosés, enriching the diversity of its wine-type portfolio.

🫧 Crémant de Bordeaux Sparkling Wine

Traditional Method Production
  • Method: Traditional method (méthode champenoise); secondary fermentation in bottle
  • Permitted varieties: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle, Pinot Noir, etc.
  • Ageing requirement: Minimum 12 months lees contact
  • Pressing: Gentle pressing to maintain clarity
  • Quality standards: Strict yield and quality restrictions
Style Characteristics
  • Fine bubbles: Persistent, delicate mousse
  • Aromas: Citrus, green apple, bread dough
  • Palate: Fresh and crisp; balanced acidity
  • Value advantage: Better value than Champagne
  • Pairings: Aperitif, seafood, light dishes
Market Position
  • Status in France: France's second largest sparkling wine region
  • International recognition: Gaining growing international recognition
  • Quality improvement: Quality has improved significantly in recent years
  • Growth potential: Considerable room for further development

🌹 Bordeaux Rosé

Production Methods
  • Short maceration: Brief skin contact with red grape varieties
  • Direct pressing: Red grapes pressed directly to yield a pale colour
  • Saignée method: A by-product of red wine production
  • Temperature control: Cool fermentation preserves freshness
Flavour Profile
  • Colour range: Pale pink to deep pink
  • Aromas: Red berries, strawberry, floral notes
  • Palate: Fresh and crisp; prominent fruit character
  • Acidity balance: Moderate acidity; well-balanced
  • Serving temperature: 8–12°C; serve chilled
Seasonal Character
  • Summer essential: Refreshing and thirst-quenching; suits hot weather
  • Outdoor activities: An excellent choice for picnics and barbecues
  • Versatile pairings: Mediterranean cuisine, Asian dishes
  • Social occasions: A relaxed, convivial party wine

🟫 Bordeaux Clairet

Historical Tradition
  • Ancient tradition: A classic wine style dating back to the medieval period
  • British preference: Was once the mainstream wine in the British market
  • Revival: Has attracted renewed interest in recent years
  • Cultural significance: Represents Bordeaux's winemaking heritage
Style Definition
  • Colour depth: Deeper than rosé; positioned between rosé and a light red
  • Maceration time: Extended skin contact of 24–48 hours
  • Flavour character: More red-fruit aromas and tannin presence
  • Serving: Can be served at room temperature or lightly chilled

📊 Wine Type Overview

Production Distribution
  • Red wines: 85% (across all quality tiers)
  • Dry white wines: 10% (mainly in Graves)
  • Sweet wines: 3% (Sauternes, Barsac, etc.)
  • Sparkling wines: 1.5% (Crémant de Bordeaux)
  • Rosé wines: 0.5% (seasonal production)
Quality Hierarchy
  • Top estates: Classified growths, garage wines, etc.
  • Quality estates: Star châteaux, artisan producers
  • Village level: Individual village AOC wines
  • Regional level: Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur AOC
slides.9.quiz.question: What production method does Crémant de Bordeaux use?
slides.9.quiz.explanation: Crémant de Bordeaux is produced using the traditional method (also known as the méthode champenoise), with secondary fermentation in bottle to create the bubbles. A minimum of 12 months lees contact is required.
slides.10.title: Lesson Complete
slides.10.description: Congratulations on completing this comprehensive study of Bordeaux's Right Bank and white wine appellations! You have now mastered the Merlot world of Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, the noble-rot sweet whites of Sauternes, and the dry whites of Entre-Deux-Mers. From the supple roundness of the Right Bank to the rich complexity of sweet whites, you now appreciate the full diversity of Bordeaux wine — not only the powerful Left Bank reds but also the beautiful Right Bank and its captivating white wines.
